inline.s: [Each mark in mutual accord, far from all the faults of views] As to the vast array of all phenomena, one should bring each mark into accord with its real nature, and so be far from the faults of the views of the two extremes. This is the signless dharma: returning the marks to the essence, apart from marks within the marks — within all marks, apart from all marks. [The faults of views] The various questions above are all views of the two extremes; with respect to entering the self-awakened noble wisdom they are all not right views, and so are called faults. The Buddha-Treasury Sutra says:
“The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is without thought and without thought-moment.”
“Pulling out the very root of all idle talk, eternally separated from all of it, cool and smokeless.”

[The siddhanta of the first meaning] The fourth of the four siddhantas; this is the ultimate siddhanta. The Buddha, seeing that the faculties and conditions of beings are ripe, speaks to them of the real nature of all dharmas, so that beings may together awaken into the path of the noble ones.
[These one hundred eight phrases, as the Buddhas have spoken] The Tang translation says:

'As the former Buddhas have said, the one hundred eight phrases, each mark in mutual accord, far from all the faults of views, also apart from the worldly dharmas made of words. I shall speak them for you; the Buddha's sons should listen and receive.' At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, what are the one hundred eight phrases?' The Buddha said to Mahamati: 'What is called the birth-phrase, the not-birth phrase; the eternal phrase, the not-eternal phrase......'

From this we know that the one hundred eight phrases 'as the Buddhas have spoken' refer to the great section below, 'the not-born phrase, the born phrase; the eternal phrase, the impermanent phrase.' [Establishing the phrases in due order] The dharma is, in its essence, beyond words; now the World-Honored One, at the place of wordlessness, displays through words, and so it is called 'establishing in due order.'

“One who separates from all marks is named a Buddha.”

blocks.text: Five. The Store Consciousness and the Evolving Consciousness
The Two Kinds of Arising, Abiding, and Ceasing

inline.s: [At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing do the consciousnesses have?]
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati again respectfully said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing do the consciousnesses have?
[Again said to the Buddha] Respectfully spoke again to the Buddha. Here 'to report to' (bai) is how the lower reports to the higher.

[The various consciousnesses] The eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness, manas-consciousness, alaya-consciousness). Here the eight consciousnesses are taken as a whole, referring to 'consciousness.' [Arising, abiding, and ceasing] Arising: the arising; abiding: the dwelling; ceasing: the extinction.

[The Buddha told Mahamati: The consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, not to be known by thought. The consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, namely the flowing-arising and the characteristic-arising; two kinds of abiding, namely the flowing-abiding and the characteristic-abiding; and two kinds of ceasing, namely the flowing-ceasing and the characteristic-ceasing.]

The Buddha told Mahamati: the consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which are not to be known through reckoning. They are the flowing arising-abiding-ceasing and the characteristic arising-abiding-ceasing. (That is, there are: flowing-arising, flowing-abiding, flowing-ceasing; characteristic-arising, characteristic-abiding, characteristic-ceasing.)

[Flowing arising-abiding-ceasing] The arising, abiding, and ceasing of a thought. Because it continues unbroken like the flowing stream of water, it is called the flowing arising-abiding-ceasing. [Thought] The stirring of the mind, flowing across the three times (past, present, future), is called a thought; the former thought, the later thought, thought after thought, and so on. [Characteristic arising-abiding-ceasing] The arising, abiding, and ceasing of the characteristics produced by the six senses conditioning on the six sense-objects.

“The Buddha said: Mahamati, the consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, not to be known by those who conjecture; namely the continuous-arising and the characteristic-arising, the continuous-abiding and the characteristic-abiding, the continuous-ceasing and the characteristic-ceasing.”

blocks.text: The True Aspect, the Transforming Aspect, and the Karmic Aspect

inline.s: [The consciousnesses have three kinds of aspects, namely the transforming aspect, the karmic aspect, and the true aspect.]
The consciousnesses have three kinds of aspects: the true aspect, the transforming aspect, and the karmic aspect.

[The three kinds of aspects] Before a single thought of unmindfulness arises, it is the true aspect; when a single thought has just arisen, it is the transforming aspect; when thought succeeds thought and becomes thinking, it is the karmic aspect. [The true aspect] The aspect apart from arising and ceasing, that is, the store consciousness spoken of below. [The transforming aspect] The aspect of passing from awareness into delusion, that is, the manifest consciousness spoken of below, that is, the 'three subtle' among the three subtle and six coarse. [The karmic aspect] The aspect of karma-creation, that is, the consciousness that discriminates particular things spoken of below, that is, the 'six coarse' among the three subtle and six coarse. These two (the transforming aspect and the karmic aspect) together are called the evolving consciousness.
the three subtle arise; with objects as conditions, the six coarse grow.”

This describes the process in which self-nature (consciousness), because of fundamental ignorance, passes from awareness (the store consciousness) into delusion (the evolving consciousness), and so arouses delusion, creates karma, and receives retribution. The 'three subtle and six coarse' are the nine false aspects of the flow of arising and ceasing that self-nature manifests when it falls into delusion: the karmic aspect of ignorance, the seeing aspect, and the object aspect (the seen aspect); the wisdom aspect, the continuous aspect, the grasping aspect, the name-reckoning aspect, the karma-arising aspect, and the karma-bound-suffering aspect. Of these, the first three are born of fundamental ignorance ('from a single thought of unmindfulness the three subtle arise'), and their aspects are subtle, so they are called the 'three subtle'; the last six are nourished by the object aspect as condition ('with objects as conditions the six coarse grow'), and their aspects are coarse and manifest, so they are called the 'six coarse.'

[Fundamental ignorance] Fundamental ignorance is the very first stirring of a thought. Because of this single stirring of thought, self-nature is benighted through the long night, not comprehending the true principle, and so gives rise to all the delusions and afflictions.
The process of the 'three subtle and six coarse' is:
One: the karmic aspect of ignorance. The stirring of the mind is karma, so 'unmindful stirring of the mind (the very first stirring of thought)' is called the karmic aspect of ignorance.
Two: the seeing aspect. Relying on the previous 'karmic aspect of ignorance,' when the mind stirs it can see.
Three: the object aspect (the seen aspect). Relying on the previous 'seeing aspect,' because of seeing, the objects falsely appear.
These three subtle take ignorance as their cause, and so it is also said: 'With ignorance as cause, the three subtle arise.'
One: the wisdom aspect. Relying on the previous 'object aspect,' it falsely produces deliberation and discriminates favorable and adverse, beautiful and ugly, loved and hated.
Two: the continuous aspect. Relying on the previous 'wisdom aspect,' toward the discrimination of objects it reflects and reckons, thought succeeding thought in continuity.

Three: the grasping aspect. Relying on the previous 'continuous aspect,' toward the continuous thoughts that turn ever deeper, it produces self and what belongs to self, thus forming the grasping aspect.
Four: the name-reckoning aspect. Relying on the previous 'grasping aspect,' it names the various environments, affairs, and things, forming concepts and language.
Five: the karma-arising aspect. Relying on the previous 'name-reckoning aspect,' it reflects and reckons and so creates various bodily, verbal, and mental karma.

Six: the karma-bound suffering aspect. Relying on the previous 'karma-arising aspect,' it is bound by the bodily, verbal, and mental karma it created and so experiences the bitter fruit of birth and death.
These six coarse are nourished by the object aspect as condition, and so it is said: 'With objects as conditions, the six coarse grow.'
“From delusion one creates karma; from karma one experiences suffering.”
This is the process of passing from awareness into delusion.
